books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Preamble and Declaration of Principles of the Knights of Labor (1878)

options.misconception: A Knights goal in the books, but it does not appear in this passage.
options.text: Government ownership of all railroads and telegraph lines.

options.misconception: This is about pay, while the stem asks for a change to daily life.
options.text: Higher wages won by striking against single employers.
A workday reduced to eight hours for all workers.

options.misconception: The passage asks for a check on wealth, not an end to private ownership.
options.text: An end to all private ownership of factories.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Knights did favor government ownership of railroads, but that goal is not in this passage.
rationales.B: A share of the wealth is about pay. The stem asks for a goal that changes daily life, and the eight-hour day does that.
rationales.C: The passage lists the reduction of the hours of labor to eight per day, which changes how workers spend each day.
rationales.D: The passage asks for a check on unjust accumulation, not for an end to private ownership.
rationales.general:
Sort the passage’s goals into pay and daily life.
1. A proper share of the wealth is about pay.
2. Equal pay for equal work is also about pay.
3. Banning child labor and cutting the day to eight hours change how people live each day.
4. Of the choices, only the eight-hour day is both in the passage and about daily life.
Remember: when a stem asks for a kind of goal, sort each choice by kind before picking.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: Which goal in the passage shows the Knights wanted to change workers’ daily lives, not only their pay?

stimulus.source_note: Preamble and Declaration of Principles of the Knights of Labor (1878), as printed in Terence V. Powderly, Thirty Years of Labor (1890). Public domain. Excerpts joined with ellipses.
stimulus.text: “The recent alarming development and aggression of aggregated wealth, which, unless checked, will invariably lead to the pauperization and hopeless degradation of the toiling masses, render it imperative, if we desire to enjoy the blessings of life, that a check should be placed upon its power and upon unjust accumulation, and a system adopted which will secure to the laborer the fruits of his toil. . . . To secure to the toilers a proper share of the wealth that they create; more of the leisure that rightfully belongs to them; more societary advantages; more of the benefits, privileges, and emoluments of the world. . . . The prohibition of the employment of children in workshops, mines, and factories before attaining their fourteenth year. . . . To secure for both sexes equal pay for equal work. The reduction of the hours of labor to eight per day.”
